meta.endpoint_note: /v1/completions was the briefed path and returns HTTP 200 with empty text and usage.completion_tokens 0 on this checkpoint (the raw path is a text continuation, not the chat template): 4 turns, all empty, 71.2 s each. The supervisor approved /v1/chat/completions for this experiment on 2026-11-11; it is the same engine, server and decode loop, and the same path the 12-prompt A/B (E12/E13) used.
meta.prompt: Explain, for a reader who knows what a cache is but nothing about language models, how a transformer keeps its memory of the conversation so far. Start with why the attention layer cannot simply re-read the whole prompt every time it emits a token, then describe the key and value rows it stores instead, how those rows grow with each new token, and why their size is the product of the context length and a per-position cost. Then explain the two ways that memory is usually made cheaper: sharing one set of key and value rows across several query heads, and storing the rows in a lower precision format. Say what each of those trades away, and say which of the two a serving engine can apply without touching the weights at all. Finish with the reason a serving engine cares about the difference between the memory held on the accelerator and the memory held in host RAM, why a machine with a small accelerator may still serve a long context, and name the number a user should ask for when they want to know how much context they can afford on a machine of a given size. Write flowing prose, no bullet points, no headings, and do not stop before the last point.

meta.tok_s_definition: usage.completion_tokens / wall seconds of the HTTP request (prefill of 239 prompt tokens plus 64 decoded tokens), measured client-side with time.monotonic() around the request
